situationText: Your teacher asks who wants to answer the first question. You raise your hand and say, "___ want to answer!" Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Oops! You're the one volunteering to answer. You're not asking your classmate to answer for you!
Nice try, but you're talking about yourself here. That pronoun would make it sound like you're talking about another person!

situationText: Your classmate is sitting beside you during an activity. You ask, "___ have a pencil I can borrow?" Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, you're asking your classmate for a pencil. You're not talking about yourself in this question!
Wait! You're talking to one classmate sitting beside you, not the whole class!

situationText: Your brother is chosen as the team captain for your school's basketball game. You tell your friend, "___ is our team captain." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, check the situation again! You're describing the team captain, so bringing the speaker into the sentence changes the meaning.
The team has one captain in this sentence, not a whole group of captains!

situationText: Your sister wins first place in the school's drawing contest. You proudly tell your classmate, "___ won the contest!" Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Nice try! The sentence is talking about someone else who won the contest, not the person speaking.
Hmm, only one person won the contest here, so check who the sentence is describing!

situationText: You and your seatmate are cleaning your classroom before dismissal. You say, "___ are cleaning our area." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Wait! You're cleaning together with your seatmate. You're part of the group, too!
Almost! You aren't cleaning alone—your seatmate is helping you with the area.

situationText: You see three of your classmates practicing for the school program. You tell your teacher, "___ are practicing outside." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, you're watching them practice from the side. You aren't part of their practice group!
Oops! There are three classmates practicing outside, not just one student!

situationText: Your teacher returns your notebook after checking your work. You reach for it and say, "Please give ___ my notebook." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Oops! Look at where the pronoun goes. You're receiving the notebook, so this form doesn't fit after 'give'.
Wait! That notebook belongs to you, not to a group of students waiting for their notebooks!

situationText: Your group is waiting outside the classroom because the teacher has not opened the door yet. Your classmate says, "Please wait for ___." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, check the spot after 'wait for.' This form doesn't sound right when someone is waiting for a group!
Oops! You're talking about your own group waiting outside, not another group of people!

situationText: Your friends are waiting for you near the school gate. You tell your older sister, "Please meet ___ there." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Nice try! Look at the word after 'meet.' That form doesn't fit when you're talking about the friends you're going to meet.
Wait! Your friends are the ones waiting at the gate. You're not asking your sister to meet your own group!

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the action word for eating in an earlier lesson. At lunch, you point to yourself and say, "___ eat my baon at recess." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, the sentence is about your own lunch routine. You're not talking directly to your classmate here!
Oops! You're the one eating your baon, not another student.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the action word for drinking in an earlier lesson. Your teacher asks what you and your seatmate do during break. You say, "___ drink water during break." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Almost! Your seatmate is drinking water with you, so you're not talking about only yourself.
Wait! You and your seatmate are part of the group you're talking about. You're not describing other students!

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the action word for going in an earlier lesson. Your friends are heading to the school canteen without you. You tell your teacher, "___ go to the canteen after class." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, you're not going with them this time. Including yourself would change who is doing the action!
Oops! You're talking about your friends, not speaking directly to the people you're talking about.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the action word for sleeping in an earlier lesson. Your little brother is already in bed. You tell your mother, "___ sleep early tonight." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Nice try! You're talking about your little brother here, but that pronoun doesn't fit the person you're describing.
Hmm, only your little brother is being described here. There's no group going to sleep.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the linking verb for a present condition in an earlier lesson. Before your class presentation, you look at your friend and say, "___ nervous today." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Oops! You're looking at your friend and talking directly to them, not describing your own feelings.
Wait! You're talking to one friend standing in front of you, not several classmates.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the linking verb for a present condition in an earlier lesson. Your sister is wearing her new school uniform. You tell your mother, "___ ready for school." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, you're talking about your sister here, but that pronoun doesn't fit the person you're describing.
Oops! Only your sister is ready for school in this situation, not a whole group.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned the linking verb for a present condition in an earlier lesson. You and your groupmates are ready to present your project. You tell the teacher, "___ ready to present." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Wait! You're part of the group presenting the project. You can't leave yourself out!
Almost! You're presenting with your groupmates, so you're definitely not the only person who is ready.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned how to count in an earlier lesson. There are three pencils on your desk, and you point to them. You say, "___ are on my desk." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Oops! You're pointing to three pencils, not one person or one thing.
Hmm, you're talking about the pencils on your desk. You aren't included in the group being described!

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned how to count in an earlier lesson. You have two notebooks, and your friend asks who they belong to. You point to yourself and say, "Those are ___." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Wait! The two notebooks belong to you, not to the friend you're talking to.
Oops! The notebooks belong to one person, not to a group of students.

situationText: [MEMORY] You learned how to count in an earlier lesson. There are five students in your group, and your teacher asks who will present. You say, "___ will present together." Which pronoun should you use?

distractors.feedback: Hmm, you're talking about your own group, and you're one of the students presenting too!
Almost! Five students are presenting together, so this isn't something one person will do alone.
